One-sentence assessment: child, family, and school social workers do not merely “persuade people”; they provide social services and assistance to improve the social and psychological functioning of children and their families and maximize family well-being and children's academic functioning. The official scope is: “Provide social services and assistance to improve the social and psychological functioning of children and their families and to maximize the family well-being and the academic functioning of children. May assist parents, arrange adoptions, and find foster homes for abandoned or abused children. In schools, they address such problems as teenage pregnancy, misbehavior, and truancy. May also advise teachers”. Daily work involves maintaining case histories and writing reports (importance 89); interviewing clients individually, as families, or in groups and assessing their circumstances, capabilities, and problems to identify needed services (87); serving as liaison among students, families, schools, family service agencies, child guidance clinics, courts, protective services, and physicians (84); developing and reviewing service plans with clients and following up to assess the quantity and quality of services (82); addressing legal issues such as child abuse and discipline, assisting at hearings, and testifying to explain custody arrangements (81); counseling parents on child-rearing and interviewing children and families to determine whether further action is needed (81); consulting parents, teachers, and other school personnel to identify causes of truancy and misbehavior and implement solutions (81); arranging medical, psychiatric, and other examinations to identify causes of difficulties and indicate remedies (80); referring clients to community resources for job placement, debt counseling, legal aid, housing, medical care, or financial assistance (75); counseling individuals, groups, families, or communities on mental health, poverty, unemployment, substance abuse, physical abuse, rehabilitation, social adjustment, child care, or medical care (75); providing, finding, or arranging support services such as child care, homemaking, prenatal care, substance abuse treatment, vocational training, counseling, or parenting classes to prevent more serious problems (75); and collecting supplementary information needed to help clients, such as employment records, medical records, or school reports (75). Supplemental tasks include placing children in foster or adoptive homes, institutions, or medical treatment centers (92); recommending temporary foster care and guiding foster or adoptive parents (88); counseling students whose behavior, academic progress, or physical or mental disabilities indicate a need for help, diagnosing problems, and arranging services (84); evaluating foster or adoption applicants (81); conducting social research (79); supervising other social workers (74); leading group counseling sessions (69); serving on policymaking committees (68); and determining clients' eligibility for financial assistance (60). O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed), with an SVP range from 7.0 to below 8.0 and interest code S (Social). Reported education is bachelor's degree 69%, master's degree 26%, and associate's or other two-year degree 6%. The central boundary: this helping role centers on assessment, service planning, coordination, and documentation, rather than clinical diagnosis or judicial rulings. This page does not present US state licensing and clinical qualification requirements as universal requirements, or mainland China's social work and child protection systems as a uniform entry threshold.

Signals for further exploration: you can stay steady and maintain boundaries in emotionally intense conversations, and are willing to document every interview and coordination activity for review. O*NET work context responses show that 100% use email daily, 95% have constant contact with others, 95% have face-to-face discussions daily, 95% have telephone conversations daily, 77% consider teamwork extremely important, 63% encounter conflict daily, 58% deal with unpleasant, angry, or discourteous people daily, 58% face time pressure daily, 52% consider dealing with external customers or the public extremely important, and 52% consider precision or accuracy extremely important. 48% have considerable freedom in making decisions, 48% have considerable freedom in setting tasks and priorities, and 43% typically work more than 40 hours per week. 48% consider the consequences of error extremely serious and 14% very serious; 19% deal with violent or physically aggressive people daily and 38% at least weekly. Work is highly automated for 14%, moderately automated for 19%, and not automated at all for 56%. These figures indicate that much of the work involves communication, assessment, and documentation; emotional and safety pressures are real and are managed through supervision, boundaries, and documentation systems.

Conditions for pausing major investment: you have not completed a supervised practice cycle of “case intake and checking information sources → interviewing and assessing needs and risks → setting service plans and goals → coordinating resources and referrals → following up and assessing service quality → documentation and supervisory review”; or you cannot remain steady and maintain professional boundaries in emotionally intense or adversarial conversations; or you are unwilling to document cases and actions according to standards and report risks through required procedures. Do not overlook risk identification and institutional constraints simply because you “like helping others”: addressing legal issues such as child abuse and assisting at hearings is an important task in this occupation. If you prefer clinical assessment and treatment, clinical and counseling psychologists and mental health social workers are related roles with different qualification requirements.

Check education, qualifications, and authorization separately: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed), with an SVP range from 7.0 to below 8.0. Education responses on its page are bachelor's degree 69%, master's degree 26%, and associate's or other two-year degree 6%. In the US, social workers generally need a bachelor's or master's degree and may need a state-issued licence; specific requirements vary by state. Clinical social workers additionally need a master's degree, supervised clinical experience, and state licensure. In mainland China, social work and child protection roles may involve social worker professional proficiency assessment, protection of minors, adoption registration, and school mental health systems; confirm applicable laws and local rules. This page does not extend one jurisdiction's licensing or registration requirements to another or present training certificates as qualifications to practise. Educational background, professional certification, statutory qualifications and qualifications to practise, and institutional authorization are four separate matters.

In one sentence: this role turns “whether needs assessments have a basis, service plans have goals and follow-up, risks are identified and reported through procedures, resource coordination is implemented, and records can be reviewed by a supervisor” into reviewable evidence. Outputs include case records, assessments and service plans; referral and coordination records; follow-up and outcome assessment records; risk identification, reporting and handover records; foster care and adoption assessment and placement records; group and parent counseling records; and policy and committee participation records. It is not a clinical diagnosis or judicial ruling role and does not replace psychiatrists, courts, or social assistance approval authorities in making final determinations on diagnosis, custody, or benefits.

The work of child, family, and school social workers has three connected but distinct areas. First, assessment and interviewing: after intake, check information sources, interview children, parents, or teachers, assess needs and risks (including safety and abuse risks), and determine whether further examination or emergency action is needed. Second, service planning and resource coordination: develop service plans and goals with clients, refer or arrange support services (child care, counseling, treatment, vocational training, etc.), and liaise among families, schools, and agencies. Third, documentation, follow-up, and supervision: maintain case histories and write reports, follow up to assess service quantity and quality, report risks through required procedures, and undergo supervisory review. All three rely on assessment evidence, plan goals, and traceable records. Authority to act differs: emergency safety action and compulsory measures are determined by statutory agencies and procedures.
Interview and assess children's and families' needs and risks, establishing a basis for judgments

Take a case and check referral sources and existing records → interview children, parents, or teachers and observe environments and interactions → organize needs, resources, and risks against an assessment framework → identify signs of safety and abuse risks → take initial measures within authorization and determine whether reporting or handover is needed → document the assessment process and its basis
Develop and review service plans, coordinate resources, and make referrals

Clarify goals and priorities with the client → choose and arrange support services and explain options and limitations → contact partners in schools, health care, justice, and social assistance and confirm responsibilities → set a follow-up schedule and contact methods → follow up and assess service quantity and quality → document coordination and service outcomes

Maintain case histories and write reports documenting interview points, assessment evidence, service plans, and follow-up results; report risks and unusual events according to procedures and deadlines and retain reporting records; assist at hearings and provide testimony within authorization for matters involving legal proceedings; strictly protect case privacy and protected information, avoiding discussion or transmission through uncontrolled channels.

Common related roles include social and community service managers, clinical and counseling psychologists, school psychologists, substance abuse and behavioral disorder counselors, and educational, guidance, and career counselors and advisors. The key boundary is not the title, but “who is qualified to diagnose and treat, who is responsible for statutory decisions such as custody and benefits, and who bears responsibility for case coordination and documentation”.
Assess needs and risks and coordinate resources to improve children's and families' functioning
Core outputs are traceable records of case assessment, service planning, coordination, and follow-up
Based on interview observations, existing records, assessment frameworks, statutory procedures, and institutional rules

US clinical and counseling psychologists focus on psychological assessment, diagnosis, and treatment; social workers focus on social services, needs assessment, coordination, and follow-up. Licensed clinical social workers may also provide treatment within state permissions. In China, mental disorder diagnosis requires a licensed psychiatrist; US occupational authority is not transplanted.

Intake and interviewing, needs and risk assessment, service planning, resource referral and liaison, follow-up and outcome assessment, documentation and supervisory review, and assistance with court proceedings

School psychologists assess and intervene in educational, behavioral, and developmental issues and may consult students, families, and school staff; this occupation emphasizes family/school social services, referrals, and follow-up. Duties may overlap.
Case records and assessments, service plans and follow-up records, referral and partner liaison records, risk reporting and handover records, and family-school communication records
Substance abuse counselors focus on addiction assessment and treatment; this occupation covers children's and families' comprehensive needs

US clinical social workers with the relevant state licence may diagnose and treat mental, behavioral, and emotional problems within their permitted scope; nonclinical social workers do not gain that authority through their occupational title. Article 29 of China's Mental Health Law requires mental disorder diagnosis by licensed psychiatrists; Articles 23/51 distinguish psychological counseling, psychotherapy, and medical authority. A social worker certificate does not automatically confer US clinical authority. Articles 92–95 of China's Law on the Protection of Minors provide for temporary/long-term guardianship by civil affairs authorities and adoption assessments; not all placement and adoption decisions are described as court decisions. Assistance eligibility determinations depend on specific authorization; O*NET supplemental tasks include determining financial assistance eligibility.

China's 2006 social worker professional proficiency assessment framework uses certificates to demonstrate professional capability, which is not equivalent to employment, medical authority, or statutory placement authority. The 2026 opinion on professional personnel issued by the two General Offices calls for expanding school/medical social work, classifying positions, improving qualifications and certificate registration, and considering qualifications, education, experience, performance, and position in pay. This is a policy direction, not a uniform individual wage or employment guarantee. Check the responsible authority's requirements for the relevant year and target role.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether information sources are reliable; whether risk signals require immediate reporting; whether service plans have clear goals and follow-up; whether resource coordination has concrete arrangements; whether records are complete and protect privacy; and whether your actions fall within your authorization and capability.
Judgment one: are information sources reliable?

Label sources for key facts, distinguish statements, observations, and confirmed findings, and cross-check when needed; reporting suspected harm is not conditional on completing verification first. Article 11 of China's Law on the Protection of Minors (amended 2024) requires state organs, residents'/villagers' committees, organizations in close contact with minors, and their staff who discover harm, suspected harm, or other danger at work to report immediately to relevant public security, civil affairs, education, or other authorities. Do not wait for confirmation or supervisory approval; internal reporting does not replace statutory reporting. Check other jurisdictions separately.
Judgment two: do risk signals require immediate reporting?

Article 11 of China's Law on the Protection of Minors (amended 2024) requires state organs, residents'/villagers' committees, organizations in close contact with minors, and their staff who discover harm, suspected harm, or other danger at work to report immediately to relevant public security, civil affairs, education, or other authorities. Do not wait for confirmation or supervisory approval; internal reporting does not replace statutory reporting. Check other jurisdictions separately.
Judgment three: does the service plan have clear goals and follow-up?
Plans should specify goals, responsible people, timing, and assessment methods. A service list without follow-up arrangements cannot support outcome assessment; supplement or adjust it during review.
Judgment four: does resource coordination have concrete arrangements?

Confirm whether the partner has accepted the referral, whether timing and conditions are clear, and whether the client must prepare additional materials; distinguish and document “referred” from “implemented”.
Judgment five: are records complete and do they protect privacy?

Records should include time, participants, facts and observations, the basis for judgments, and next steps; restrict access according to institutional and jurisdictional requirements, and do not discuss or transmit case information through uncontrolled channels.
Judgment six: are actions within authorization and capability?

Refer services beyond your qualifications/capabilities to appropriate professionals and seek supervisory support concurrently if needed; urgent safety risks and statutory reporting must not wait for supervisory approval. Article 11 of China's Law on the Protection of Minors (amended 2024) requires state organs, residents'/villagers' committees, organizations in close contact with minors, and their staff who discover harm, suspected harm, or other danger at work to report immediately to relevant public security, civil affairs, education, or other authorities. Do not wait for confirmation or supervisory approval; internal reporting does not replace statutory reporting. Check other jurisdictions separately.

They may assist parents, arrange adoptions, and find foster homes for abandoned or abused children; in schools, they address teenage pregnancy, misbehavior, and truancy and may advise teachers (official O*NET-SOC 21-1021.00 scope). A social worker certificate does not automatically confer US clinical authority. Articles 92–95 of China's Law on the Protection of Minors provide for temporary/long-term guardianship by civil affairs authorities and adoption assessments; not all placement and adoption decisions are described as court decisions. Assistance eligibility determinations depend on specific authorization; O*NET supplemental tasks include determining financial assistance eligibility. paragraphs: The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: listening and communication, needs judgments, documentation and collaboration, and familiarity with systems and procedures. Differences concern qualifications (authority for diagnosis/treatment or statutory investigation), service users (children/families versus adult addiction or academic guidance), and responsibility (service coordination versus clinical/statutory decisions). Before comparing titles, test the choice through an assessment and service plan you can deliver.

The comparison draws on task and work activity descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 21-1021.00 page, related occupations registered in this entry's evidence routing (social-and-community-service-managers, clinical-and-counseling-psychologists, school-psychologists, substance-abuse-and-behavioral-disorder-counselors, educational-guidance-and-career-counselors-and-advisors), and editorial explanations of role boundaries. Entry requirements, qualifications to practise, and statutory authority must be checked separately against each role's own page and local law; this table does not prescribe professional or statutory duties.

The table compares related roles and occupations: social and community service managers, clinical and counseling psychologists, school psychologists, substance abuse and behavioral disorder counselors, educational, guidance, and career counselors and advisors, and child protection and placement roles. Its four columns address the same kinds of questions: what each direction does, its key differences from this occupation, and who may be better suited to choose it.

Social and community service managers handle organization, resource allocation, and performance management; this occupation's frontline duties are assessment, service coordination, and follow-up. Management is usually a role after advancement.

People seeking team and project management are suited to the social and community service manager direction; those willing to do frontline assessment and coordination over the long term are suited to this occupation.
Manage and coordinate social service programs, teams, and budgets; outputs mainly concern program performance, team reports, and compliance reports.
Social and community service managers

Clinical and counseling psychologists are qualified to diagnose and treat and are responsible for treatment outcomes; this occupation handles needs assessment, service planning, and resource coordination, without diagnosis or treatment.
People wanting to diagnose and treat are suited to clinical and counseling psychology; those wanting to coordinate services in family and school settings are suited to this occupation.
Provide psychological assessment, diagnosis, and treatment; outputs mainly comprise diagnoses, treatment plans, and records.
Clinical and counseling psychologists
School psychologists mainly conduct psychological testing and academic interventions; this occupation mainly assesses needs, coordinates services, and follows up in family and school settings.
People preferring testing and teaching/learning interventions are suited to school psychology; those preferring family and multiagency coordination are suited to this occupation.
Provide psychological testing and academic and behavioral interventions in schools; outputs mainly comprise assessment reports and intervention plans.
School psychologists

Substance abuse counselors address addiction and behavioral disorders and need relevant qualifications to practise; this occupation covers children's and families' comprehensive needs and bears coordination responsibilities.
People wanting to provide addiction treatment are suited to substance abuse counseling; those wanting to provide comprehensive services to children and families are suited to this occupation.
Provide addiction and behavioral disorder assessment, counseling, and treatment plans; outputs mainly comprise treatment plans and counseling records.
Substance abuse and behavioral disorder counselors
Educational, guidance, and career counselors and advisors address academic and career choices; this occupation covers broader issues including safety, family functioning, and legal procedures.
People preferring further-education and career planning guidance are suited to educational guidance; those willing to address family and risk issues are suited to this occupation.
Provide academic, further-education, and career guidance in schools; outputs mainly comprise guidance records and planning proposals.
Educational, guidance, and career counselors and advisors
These roles generally have statutory investigation and compulsory action powers; this occupation assists with statutory procedures and provides services and records within authorization.
People wanting to investigate and take compulsory action under statutory powers are suited to child protection roles; those wanting service and coordination work are suited to this occupation.
Conduct child protection investigations, placements, and guardianship assistance within statutory agencies; outputs mainly comprise investigation, action, and placement records.
Child protection and placement roles

If you prefer clinical diagnosis and treatment, compare clinical and counseling psychologists further; if you prefer school testing and academic intervention, compare school psychologists; if you focus on addiction and behavioral disorder treatment, compare substance abuse and behavioral disorder counselors; if you prefer project management or statutory investigation, compare social and community service managers or child protection and placement roles respectively. Their qualifications to practise and authority structures differ from this occupation; do not confuse this page's service and coordination judgments with clinical or statutory decisions.

values: Fictional scenario: a fictional community service agency receives a referral about a 9-year-old student recently absent frequently and with unexplained injuries. Provided materials are fictional institutional intake procedures and risk reporting points and a fictional school/family background summary.
Fictional materials: a record of statements from a teacher, parent, and neighbor (with two factual inconsistencies) and a fictional prior service record.

Fictional resource list: community resources for psychological counseling, after-school care, financial assistance, and legal aid (including acceptance conditions, contacts, and material requirements).
Fictional conditions: fictional home-visit safety procedures and supervisor contact details.
Step one: use intake procedures to write an intake checklist listing facts and information sources requiring verification, and explain the basis for each step.
Step two: write risk assessment points (including the basis for reporting/handover decisions under procedures) and explain the verification order when the three statements disagree.
Step three: design service plan points and follow-up arrangements for the student (goals, responsible parties, timing), select suitable referrals from the resource list, and explain why.
Suggested deliverables: an intake checklist with its basis, a risk assessment and reporting decision explanation, and a table of service plan, referral, and follow-up points.

Assessment basis: whether checklist items match institutional processes, distinguish “can follow up yourself” from “must report or hand over through procedures”, and include traceable information such as time, sources, facts, and judgment evidence.
Multiple reasonable approaches are allowed; if some information is insufficient for judgment, clearly specify what cannot be judged and what additional information is needed.
